        PLACEMENT_NAME=$(echo $placement | cut -d'/' -f2)

  • Proposed Fix: 

    # Check Placements (RHACM 2.6+)
echo "🔍 Checking placements..."
PLACEMENTS=$(oc get placement -n $POLICY_NAMESPACE -o name 2>/dev/null || true)
if [ -z "$PLACEMENTS" ]; then
    echo -e "${YELLOW}⚠ No placements found${NC}"
else
    for placement in $PLACEMENTS; do
        PLACEMENT_NAME=$(echo $placement | cut -d'/' -f2)
        # Check PlacementDecisions (not decisions in Placement status)
        DECISIONS=$(oc get placementdecision -n $POLICY_NAMESPACE -l cluster.open-cluster-management.io/placement=$PLACEMENT_NAME -o json 2>/dev/null | jq -r '.items[].status.decisions // []' || echo "[]")

  • Explanation: Changed from deprecated placementrule to modern placement API, and updated to check PlacementDecision resources instead of inline status.decisions.

docs.title: 1. Missing Unavailable Tolerations (Widespread)
docs.text:
Pattern: 14 out of 18 Placement objects across all examples are missing the cluster.open-cluster-management.io/unavailable toleration.

Why This Matters: - RHACM 2.15+ best practices explicitly recommend BOTH unreachable and unavailable tolerations - unreachable: Cluster cannot be contacted (network issue, cluster down) - unavailable: Cluster is contactable but not ready (upgrading, degraded state) - Without unavailable toleration, policies are removed during cluster upgrades or maintenance windows

Fix Pattern: Add this to ALL Placements: 

tolerations:
- key: cluster.open-cluster-management.io/unreachable
  operator: Exists
- key: cluster.open-cluster-management.io/unavailable
  operator: Exists

Affected Files: 1. 1_basic_secret_distribution/placement-all-clusters.yaml 2. 1_basic_secret_distribution/placement-production.yaml (3 Placements) 3. 2_managed_service_accounts/placement-prod-clusters.yaml 4. 3_external_secrets_operator/placement-binding.yaml (2 Placements) 5. 4_registry_credentials/placement-binding.yaml (2 Placements) 6. 5_database_secrets/placement-binding.yaml (3 Placements) 7. 6_advanced_patterns/placement-binding.yaml (1 Placement) 8. 6_advanced_patterns/managedclusterset-placement.yaml (2 Placements)

docs.title: 2. Inconsistent Toleration Patterns
docs.text:
Observation: Some Placement objects have both tolerations (like 6_advanced_patterns/placement-binding.yaml production-clusters), while most have only unreachable. This inconsistency makes it unclear whether the unavailable toleration is optional or required.

Recommendation: Standardize on BOTH tolerations for ALL Placements to match RHACM 2.15+ best practices documented in RHACM-2.15-BEST-PRACTICES.md.

docs.title: 3. Excellent API Version Compliance
docs.text:
Positive Finding: ALL YAML files correctly use: - cluster.open-cluster-management.io/v1beta1 for Placement - cluster.open-cluster-management.io/v1beta2 for ManagedClusterSet and ManagedClusterSetBinding - policy.open-cluster-management.io/v1 for Policy and PlacementBinding

No deprecated apps.open-cluster-management.io/v1 PlacementRule usage was found in actual YAML files.

docs.title: 1. Hub Secret References
docs.text:
✅ Excellent Implementation - The examples correctly demonstrate Hub secret references with proper syntax: 

DB_PASSWORD: '{{hub fromSecret "rhacm-secrets" "prod-database" "password" hub}}'

All Hub secret template usage follows RHACM 2.8+ specifications.

docs.title: 2. ManagedClusterSet Architecture
docs.text:

docs.title: 3. Security Practices

docs.title: Distribute Resources Across Managed Clusters with RHACM
docs.text: Audience: Platform engineers, SREs, or anyone managing multiple OCP clusters through RHACM Purpose: Practical guide to pushing a resource definition to all managed clusters using RHACM's policy framework

docs.title: The Problem
docs.text: You have a YAML file — a ConfigMap, Secret, NetworkPolicy, CustomResource — and you want it applied to every cluster under RHACM's management. Three paths exist, from quick-and-dirty to production-grade.

docs.title: Option 1: Direct oc Loop (One-Off Only)
docs.text:
For a single deployment with no ongoing drift control:

for cluster in $(oc get managedclusters -o jsonpath='{.items[?(@.metadata.name!="local-cluster")].metadata.name}'); do
  oc --context=${cluster} -n <namespace> apply -f your-resource.yaml
done

Why this is a dead end: If someone edits a resource directly on a managed cluster, nothing corrects it. You're managing by memory, not by state. Use this for the initial bootstrap; switch to Option 2 for everything after.

docs.title: Option 2: RHACM Policy + Placement (Recommended)
docs.text:
This is the RHACM-native approach. Three resources work together:

Resource Role Placement Defines which clusters get the resource PlacementBinding Wires the Policy to the Placement Policy Wraps your YAML as a ConfigurationPolicy

RHACM continuously reconciles. If a resource is deleted or modified on any managed cluster, it gets put back.

docs.title: Step 1: Placement — Select Clusters
docs.text:
apiVersion: cluster.open-cluster-management.io/v1beta1
kind: Placement
metadata:
  name: all-managed-clusters
  namespace: rhacm-policies
spec:
  predicates:
  - requiredClusterSelector:
      matchExpressions:
      - key: name
        operator: NotIn
        values:
        - local-cluster
  tolerations:
  - key: cluster.open-cluster-management.io/unreachable
    operator: Exists
  - key: cluster.open-cluster-management.io/unavailable
    operator: Exists

This selects every managed cluster except the local hub cluster. The tolerations prevent policies from vanishing during transient network issues — add both unreachable and unavailable for resilience.

If you want to scope to a subset, use labels instead:

spec:
  predicates:
  - requiredClusterSelector:
      labelSelector:
        matchLabels:
          environment: production

See placement-by-labels.yaml for filtering patterns (AND logic, NOT-in exclusions, multi-value OR, label existence checks, MergedPredicate).

docs.title: Step 2: PlacementBinding — Wire Policy to Placement
docs.text:
apiVersion: policy.open-cluster-management.io/v1
kind: PlacementBinding
metadata:
  name: binding-all-clusters
  namespace: rhacm-policies
placementRef:
  name: all-managed-clusters
  kind: Placement
  apiGroup: cluster.open-cluster-management.io
subjects:
- name: my-resource-policy
  kind: Policy
  apiGroup: policy.open-cluster-management.io

This connects the policy to the placement. The placementRef must reference a Placement (not a PlacementRule — those are deprecated as of RHACM 2.15+).

docs.title: Step 3: Policy — Wrap Your YAML
docs.text:
apiVersion: policy.open-cluster-management.io/v1
kind: Policy
metadata:
  name: my-resource-policy
  namespace: rhacm-policies
spec:
  remediationAction: enforce
  disabled: false
  policy-templates:
  - objectDefinition:
      apiVersion: policy.open-cluster-management.io/v1
      kind: ConfigurationPolicy
      metadata:
        name: my-resource-config
      spec:
        remediationAction: enforce
        severity: high
        namespaceSelector:
          include:
          - <your-namespace>
        object-templates:
        - complianceType: musthave
          objectDefinition:
            # Paste your YAML here, verbatim
            apiVersion: v1
            kind: ConfigMap
            metadata:
              name: my-config
              namespace: <your-namespace>
            data:
              key: value

The critical fields: - remediationAction: enforce — this is what drives drift correction. inform would report but not fix. - complianceType: musthave — the resource must exist with these exact properties. - namespaceSelector.include — which namespace(s) on managed clusters to target.

docs.title: Apply and Verify
docs.text:
# Apply all three to the hub
oc apply -f placement-all-clusters.yaml
oc apply -f binding-all-clusters.yaml
oc apply -f policy-my-resource.yaml

# Verify which clusters are targeted
oc get placementdecision -n rhacm-policies
oc get placementdecision -l cluster.open-cluster-management.io/placement=all-managed-clusters -o yaml

# Check policy status
oc get policies -n rhacm-policies -o wide

docs.title: Option 3: GitOps with ArgoCD — For Existing GitOps Pipelines
docs.text: If you're using ArgoCD, you can register RHACM-managed clusters as ArgoCD targets and deploy applications via ApplicationSet driven by cluster labels. The repo is your source of truth; ArgoCD handles deployment and drift correction.

docs.title: Registering RHACM Clusters with ArgoCD
docs.text:
ArgoCD can discover clusters through RHACM using either:

ManagedClusterSet binding (RHACM → ArgoCD integration):

# In the openshift-gitops namespace
apiVersion: cluster.open-cluster-management.io/v1beta2
kind: ManagedClusterSetBinding
metadata:
  name: default
spec:
  clusterSet: default
---
apiVersion: cluster.open-cluster-management.io/v1beta1
kind: Placement
metadata:
  name: all-openshift-clusters
  namespace: openshift-gitops
spec:
  clusterSets:
  - default
  predicates:
  - requiredClusterSelector:
      labelSelector:
        matchExpressions:
        - key: vendor
          operator: In
          values:
          - OpenShift
---
apiVersion: apps.open-cluster-management.io/v1beta1
kind: GitOpsCluster
metadata:
  name: argo-acm-clusters
  namespace: openshift-gitops
spec:
  argoServer:
    cluster: local-cluster
    argoNamespace: openshift-gitops
  placementRef:
    kind: Placement
    apiVersion: cluster.open-cluster-management.io/v1beta1
    name: all-openshift-clusters

This is a one-time setup on the hub — after applying it, ArgoCD automatically discovers managed clusters as deployment destinations.

docs.title: Deploying with ApplicationSet
docs.text:
Once clusters are registered, use ApplicationSet with the cluster selector:

apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: ApplicationSet
metadata:
  name: global-config
  namespace: openshift-gitops
spec:
  generators:
  - list:
      elements:
      - cluster: local-cluster
        namespace: kube-system
      - cluster: cluster-a
        namespace: default
      - cluster: cluster-b
        namespace: default
  template:
    metadata:
      name: '{{cluster}}-config'
    spec:
      project: default
      source:
        repoURL: https://github.com/org/gitops-repo.git
        targetRevision: main
        path: configs/{{cluster}}
      destination:
        server: https://kubernetes.default.svc
        namespace: '{{namespace}}'

For label-based cluster selection instead of a hardcoded list, combine with the ManagedClusterSet pattern above and use the cluster generator from the argocd-rbac integration.

See gitops-cluster-integration/ for the full ManagedClusterSet + ArgoCD integration examples.

docs.title: Targeting Subsets with Labels
docs.text:
For production environments, you rarely want "everything everywhere." Label your clusters consistently:

# Label clusters
oc label managedcluster cluster-1 environment=production region=us-east-1
oc label managedcluster cluster-2 environment=production region=us-west-2
oc label managedcluster cluster-3 environment=staging region=us-east-1

Then create a Placement that filters by those labels:

apiVersion: cluster.open-cluster-management.io/v1beta1
kind: Placement
metadata:
  name: production-clusters
  namespace: rhacm-policies
spec:
  predicates:
  - requiredClusterSelector:
      labelSelector:
        matchLabels:
          environment: production
  tolerations:
  - key: cluster.open-cluster-management.io/unreachable
    operator: Exists

Common label patterns: - environment: production | staging | development - region: us-east-1 | us-west-2 | eu-central-1 - cloud: aws | azure | gcp | on-prem - compliance: pci-dss | hipaa | sox

docs.title: Hub Secret References (Don't Embed Secrets in YAML)
docs.text:
For secrets, store them on the hub and reference them in policies:

# Create secret on hub
oc create secret generic db-credentials \
  -n rhacm-secrets \
  --from-literal=password=secret123

Then in your policy template:

object-templates:
- complianceType: musthave
  objectDefinition:
    apiVersion: v1
    kind: Secret
    metadata:
      name: db-credentials
      namespace: <your-namespace>
    type: Opaque
    stringData:
      password: '{{hub fromSecret "rhacm-secrets" "db-credentials" "password" hub}}'

Benefits: Single source of truth, centralized rotation, no secrets in Git. For production workloads, consider External Secrets Operator instead — it pushes secrets to Vault/AWS SM and creates ExternalSecrets on managed clusters, meaning Kubernetes never stores the secret at rest.

See the full secret management examples at secret-management/.

docs.title: Common Pitfalls
docs.text:
PlacementBinding references PlacementRule. PlacementRule is deprecated as of RHACM 2.6, removed in 2.15+. Use kind: Placement with apiGroup: cluster.open-cluster-management.io.

Missing ManagedClusterSetBinding. When using a ManagedClusterSet, you must bind it to a namespace before the Placement can use it. See placement-binding.yaml for the pattern.

No tolerations. Without tolerations, policies disappear when a cluster temporarily goes unreachable. Always add at minimum cluster.open-cluster-management.io/unreachable.

remediationAction: inform instead of enforce. inform reports drift but doesn't correct it. Use enforce if you want automatic remediation.

docs.title: ArgoCD RBAC via RHACM Policy
docs.text: This pattern uses a RHACM Policy to declaratively grant OpenShift GitOps (ArgoCD) cluster-admin permissions on managed clusters. This avoids manually applying ClusterRoleBindings and ensures they are continuously reconciled by RHACM.

docs.title: Why RHACM for RBAC?
docs.text:
• Declarative drift prevention: RHACM continuously enforces the policy. If someone removes the ClusterRoleBinding, it is automatically re-created.
  • Multi-cluster scale: A single policy propagates to all matching clusters via PlacementRule. No per-cluster manual steps.
  • Audit trail: All policy changes flow through Git, providing a clear history of who granted what and when.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• RHACM MultiClusterHub running on the hub cluster
  • OpenShift GitOps operator installed (creates the openshift-gitops namespace and service accounts)

docs.title: What the Policy Does
docs.text:
Creates two ClusterRoleBinding resources on each targeted cluster:

Binding Name Service Account Role argocd-application-controller-cluster-admin openshift-gitops-argocd-application-controller cluster-admin argocd-server-cluster-admin openshift-gitops-argocd-server cluster-admin

docs.title: Targeting
docs.text:
The included PlacementRule targets only the local hub cluster (local-cluster: "true").

To target all managed clusters, modify the PlacementRule:

spec:
  clusterConditions:
  - status: "True"
    type: ManagedClusterConditionAvailable
  clusterSelector:
    matchExpressions: []  # empty = all clusters

To target a specific set of clusters by label:

spec:
  clusterSelector:
    matchLabels:
      environment: production

docs.title: Apply
docs.text:
Once ACM's MultiClusterHub is in Running state:

oc apply -f policy-argocd-cluster-admin.yaml -n open-cluster-management

Verify the policy is compliant:

oc get policy policy-argocd-cluster-admin -n open-cluster-management

The COMPLIANT column should show Compliant once the bindings are applied on all targeted clusters.

docs.title: Verify on Target Cluster
docs.text:
oc get clusterrolebinding argocd-application-controller-cluster-admin
oc get clusterrolebinding argocd-server-cluster-admin

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• remediationAction: enforce means RHACM will create/fix the bindings automatically.
  • Changing to inform makes the policy read-only (reports compliance without taking action).
  • This is intentionally scoped to OpenShift GitOps service accounts. If you use a different ArgoCD installation namespace, update the namespace field in the subjects entries.

docs.title: RHACM Cluster Import - Ansible Automation
docs.text: Simple Ansible playbook to automate importing existing OpenShift clusters into Red Hat Advanced Cluster Management (RHACM).

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: This example implements Strategy 2: Ansible Automation from the cluster import automation strategies. It provides a single playbook that: 1. Creates ManagedCluster and KlusterletAddonConfig on the RHACM hub 2. Waits for the import secret to be generated 3. Extracts the import manifest from the secret 4. Applies the manifest to the target cluster 5. Validates the cluster is successfully imported

docs.title: Software Requirements
docs.text:
• Ansible Core 2.15+ installed on control node
  • kubernetes.core collection installed
  • oc or kubectl CLI available in PATH

docs.title: Install Ansible Collection
docs.text: ansible-galaxy collection install kubernetes.core

docs.title: Access Requirements
docs.text:
• Hub Cluster: Kubeconfig with permissions to:
  • Create ManagedCluster resources
  • Create KlusterletAddonConfig resources
  • Read secrets in cluster namespaces

Recommended: Use dedicated service account with minimal permissions - See hub-rbac/README.md for RBAC setup - Follows principle of least privilege - Better than using cluster-admin kubeconfig

  • Target Cluster: Kubeconfig with cluster-admin permissions to:
  • Create namespaces
  • Create operator resources
  • Create RBAC resources

docs.title: Network Requirements
docs.text:
• Ansible control node can reach both hub and target cluster APIs
  • Target cluster can reach hub cluster (for klusterlet → hub communication)
  • If using bastion hosts, configure SSH proxy in inventory

docs.title: 1. Configure Inventory
docs.text:
Edit inventory/hosts.ini with your cluster details:

[rhacm_hub]
hub-cluster kubeconfig_path=/path/to/hub-kubeconfig

[target_clusters]
prod-cluster-01 kubeconfig_path=/path/to/prod-cluster-01-kubeconfig

docs.title: 2. Configure Cluster Variables
docs.text:
Edit group_vars/target_clusters.yml or create host-specific vars in host_vars/:

# Cluster labels for placement and governance
cluster_labels:
  environment: production
  cloud: baremetal
  region: us-east-1

# Klusterlet add-ons to enable
klusterlet_addons:
  application_manager: true
  policy_controller: true
  search_collector: true
  cert_policy_controller: true

docs.title: 3. Run the Playbook
docs.text:
# Import a specific cluster
ansible-playbook -i inventory/hosts.ini import-cluster.yml \
  --limit prod-cluster-01

# Import all clusters in inventory
ansible-playbook -i inventory/hosts.ini import-cluster.yml

docs.title: 4. Verify Import
docs.text:
# Check ManagedCluster status on hub
oc get managedcluster prod-cluster-01

# Check conditions
oc get managedcluster prod-cluster-01 -o jsonpath='{.status.conditions[*].type}'

docs.title: Files in This Example
docs.text:
cluster-import-ansible/
├── README.md                      # This file
├── import-cluster.yml             # Main playbook
├── inventory/
│   └── hosts.ini                  # Inventory file
├── group_vars/
│   └── target_clusters.yml        # Default variables
└── host_vars/
    └── prod-cluster-01.yml        # Cluster-specific variables (example)

docs.title: Step 1: Create ManagedCluster
docs.text:
• Creates namespace on hub (same name as cluster)
  • Creates ManagedCluster resource with specified labels
  • Sets hubAcceptsClient: true

docs.title: Step 2: Create KlusterletAddonConfig
docs.text:
• Defines which add-ons to enable
  • Configures add-on settings

docs.title: Step 3: Wait for Import Secret
docs.text:
• Polls for <cluster-name>-import secret
  • Timeout: 2 minutes (configurable)
  • Retries every 5 seconds

docs.title: Step 4: Extract Import Manifest
docs.text:
• Decodes import.yaml from secret data
  • Stores in Ansible facts for delegation

docs.title: Step 5: Apply to Target Cluster
docs.text:
• Applies import manifest to target cluster
  • Creates klusterlet namespace and operators

docs.title: Step 6: Validate Import
docs.text:
• Waits for ManagedClusterJoined condition
  • Waits for ManagedClusterAvailable condition
  • Reports success or failure

docs.title: Cluster Labels
docs.text:
Add custom labels for placement and governance:

# host_vars/prod-cluster-01.yml
cluster_labels:
  environment: production
  datacenter: dc1
  rack: rack42
  owner: platform-team
  cost-center: "12345"

Labels are used by RHACM for: - Placement policies (target clusters for apps/policies) - Cluster organization and filtering - Governance and compliance reporting

docs.title: Klusterlet Add-ons
docs.text:
Enable/disable add-ons per cluster:

klusterlet_addons:
  application_manager: true      # Application lifecycle management
  policy_controller: true        # Policy enforcement
  search_collector: false        # Search indexing (disable for performance)
  cert_policy_controller: true   # Certificate policy management

docs.title: Timeout Configuration
docs.text:
Adjust timeouts in playbook variables:

# In import-cluster.yml
vars:
  import_secret_timeout_seconds: 120
  import_validation_timeout_seconds: 300

docs.title: Using Bastion/Jump Host
docs.text:
For bare metal clusters behind bastion hosts:

[target_clusters]
bm-prod-01 kubeconfig_path=/path/to/kubeconfig

[target_clusters:vars]
ansible_ssh_common_args='-o ProxyJump=bastion.example.com'

docs.title: Multiple Data Centers
docs.text:
Organize by location:

[dc_east]
east-bm-01 kubeconfig_path=/path/to/east-bm-01-kubeconfig
east-bm-02 kubeconfig_path=/path/to/east-bm-02-kubeconfig

[dc_west]
west-bm-01 kubeconfig_path=/path/to/west-bm-01-kubeconfig

[target_clusters:children]
dc_east
dc_west

Then import by data center:

ansible-playbook -i inventory/hosts.ini import-cluster.yml --limit dc_east

docs.title: Import Secret Not Generated
docs.text:
Symptom: Playbook times out waiting for import secret

Causes: - Hub cluster multicluster-engine not healthy - Insufficient RBAC permissions - Namespace creation failed

Debug: 

# Check multicluster-engine status
oc get pods -n multicluster-engine

# Check namespace exists
oc get namespace prod-cluster-01

# Check for error events
oc get events -n prod-cluster-01

docs.title: Import Manifest Application Failed
docs.text:
Symptom: Task "Apply import manifest to target cluster" fails

Causes: - Insufficient permissions on target cluster - Network connectivity issues - Target cluster API unavailable

Debug: 

# Test kubeconfig connectivity
KUBECONFIG=/path/to/target-kubeconfig oc whoami
KUBECONFIG=/path/to/target-kubeconfig oc auth can-i create namespace

# Check for existing klusterlet
KUBECONFIG=/path/to/target-kubeconfig oc get klusterlet -A

docs.title: Cluster Not Joining
docs.text:
Symptom: ManagedCluster created but never reaches Available status

Causes: - Network connectivity from target to hub blocked - Certificate issues - Hub cluster URL unreachable from target

Debug: 

# On hub: Check ManagedCluster conditions
oc get managedcluster prod-cluster-01 -o yaml

# On target: Check klusterlet pods
KUBECONFIG=/path/to/target-kubeconfig oc get pods -n open-cluster-management-agent

# On target: Check klusterlet logs
KUBECONFIG=/path/to/target-kubeconfig oc logs -n open-cluster-management-agent \
  -l app=klusterlet-registration-agent

docs.title: Parallel Import
docs.text:
Import multiple clusters in parallel using Ansible forks:

ansible-playbook -i inventory/hosts.ini import-cluster.yml --forks 5

Warning: Don't set forks too high as it can overwhelm the hub cluster.

docs.title: Dry Run
docs.text:
Check what would be created without making changes:

ansible-playbook -i inventory/hosts.ini import-cluster.yml --check

Note: Check mode has limitations - it can't predict secret generation.

docs.title: Integration with Ansible Tower/AAP
docs.text:
1. Create project pointing to this Git repository
  2. Create inventory with cluster credentials
  3. Create job template:
  4. Playbook: import-cluster.yml
  5. Credentials: Add kubeconfigs as file credentials
  6. Survey: Optional - prompt for cluster name
  7. Launch job template to import clusters on-demand

docs.title: Integration with CI/CD
docs.text:
Call from Jenkins/GitLab CI:

stage('Import Cluster to RHACM') {
    steps {
        sh '''
            ansible-playbook -i inventory/hosts.ini import-cluster.yml \
              --limit ${CLUSTER_NAME} \
              --extra-vars "cluster_name=${CLUSTER_NAME}"
        '''
    }
}

docs.title: Enable Verbose Output
docs.text: ansible-playbook -i inventory/hosts.ini import-cluster.yml -vvv

docs.title: Check Ansible Facts
docs.text:
Add debug tasks to playbook to inspect variables:

- name: Debug cluster configuration
  debug:
    msg:
      - "Cluster: {{ inventory_hostname }}"
      - "Labels: {{ cluster_labels }}"
      - "Kubeconfig: {{ kubeconfig_path }}"

docs.title: Manual Verification Steps
docs.text:
# 1. Verify ManagedCluster created
oc get managedcluster <cluster-name>

# 2. Verify import secret exists
oc get secret <cluster-name>-import -n <cluster-name>

# 3. Extract and inspect import manifest
oc get secret <cluster-name>-import -n <cluster-name> \
  -o jsonpath='{.data.import\.yaml}' | base64 -d > /tmp/import.yaml
cat /tmp/import.yaml

# 4. Check target cluster klusterlet
KUBECONFIG=/path/to/target oc get pods -n open-cluster-management-agent

# 5. Verify hub accepts connection
oc get managedcluster <cluster-name> -o yaml

docs.title: Kubeconfig Storage
docs.text:
Development/Lab: - Store kubeconfigs in filesystem with proper permissions (600) - Use Ansible Vault for sensitive inventories

Production: - Store kubeconfigs in HashiCorp Vault or similar - Use Ansible Vault lookups to retrieve dynamically - Rotate kubeconfigs regularly - Use service accounts with limited scope when possible

Example with Ansible Vault: 

kubeconfig_path: "{{ lookup('vault', 'secret/data/kubeconfigs/prod-cluster-01') }}"

docs.title: RBAC Principle of Least Privilege
docs.text:
Create service accounts with minimal required permissions:

Hub Cluster: 

apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: ClusterRole
metadata:
  name: cluster-importer
rules:
  - apiGroups: ["cluster.open-cluster-management.io"]
    resources: ["managedclusters"]
    verbs: ["create", "get", "list"]
  - apiGroups: ["agent.open-cluster-management.io"]
    resources: ["klusterletaddonconfigs"]
    verbs: ["create", "get"]
  - apiGroups: [""]
    resources: ["namespaces", "secrets"]
    verbs: ["create", "get"]

Target Cluster: - Requires cluster-admin or equivalent for klusterlet installation - Consider pre-creating namespace with limited scope service account

docs.title: Bastion Node Setup for RHACM Automation
docs.text: This guide helps set up bastion/jump hosts for RHACM cluster import automation.

docs.title: The Problem
docs.text:
When delegating Ansible tasks to a bastion node, you may encounter:

failed to import the required python library (kubernetes)

This happens because the kubernetes.core collection requires the Python kubernetes library on the node executing the task.

docs.title: Solution 1: Keep Delegation to localhost (Recommended)
docs.text: Best approach: Don't delegate Kubernetes tasks to the bastion. Instead, use SSH proxy.

docs.title: inventory/hosts.ini
docs.text:
[rhacm_hub]
hub-cluster kubeconfig_path=/path/to/hub-kubeconfig

[target_clusters]
prod-cluster-01 kubeconfig_path=/path/to/prod-cluster-01-kubeconfig

# Use SSH proxy for network access
[target_clusters:vars]
ansible_ssh_common_args='-o ProxyJump=bastion.example.com'

docs.title: How it works:
docs.text:
• Kubernetes tasks run on your Ansible control node (localhost)
  • SSH connections to target clusters tunnel through bastion
  • No Python dependencies needed on bastion
  • Cleaner separation of concerns

docs.title: Solution 2: Install Dependencies on Bastion
docs.text: If you must delegate to bastion, install required libraries:

docs.title: Manual Installation
docs.text:
System-wide (requires sudo): 

# SSH to bastion
ssh bastion.example.com

# Install pip3
sudo dnf install python3-pip -y  # RHEL/CentOS
# or
sudo apt install python3-pip -y  # Ubuntu/Debian

# Install kubernetes library (system-wide)
sudo pip3 install kubernetes

# Verify
python3 -c "import kubernetes; print(kubernetes.__version__)"

User-specific (no sudo required): 

# SSH to bastion
ssh bastion.example.com

# Install kubernetes library for current user
pip3 install --user kubernetes

# Verify
python3 -c "import kubernetes; print(kubernetes.__version__)"

# Location: ~/.local/lib/python3.x/site-packages/

docs.title: Automated Installation with Playbook
docs.text:
System-wide installation: 

# Add bastion to inventory
cat >> inventory/hosts.ini <<EOF

[bastion]
bastion.example.com ansible_user=admin
EOF

# Run setup playbook (installs for all users)
ansible-playbook -i inventory/hosts.ini bastion-setup.yml

User-specific installation: 

# Run setup playbook for current user only (no sudo)
ansible-playbook -i inventory/hosts.ini bastion-setup.yml \
  -e "install_user_only=true"

Choose the right approach: - System-wide: Good for shared bastion used by multiple users - User-specific: Good when you don't have sudo, or want isolated deps

docs.title: Solution 3: Use Container/Podman on Bastion
docs.text:
Run Ansible in a container with all dependencies:

# On bastion
podman run -it --rm \
  -v /path/to/kubeconfigs:/kubeconfigs:Z \
  -v /path/to/playbooks:/playbooks:Z \
  quay.io/ansible/ansible-runner:latest \
  ansible-playbook -i /playbooks/inventory/hosts.ini /playbooks/import-cluster.yml

docs.title: Comparison
docs.text: Approach Pros Cons SSH Proxy (localhost) ✅ No bastion dependencies✅ Simpler setup✅ Better security ⚠️ Requires SSH access from control node Install on Bastion ✅ Direct execution✅ Works in air-gapped ❌ Dependency management❌ Version conflicts Container on Bastion ✅ Isolated environment✅ Consistent deps ❌ More complex❌ Requires container runtime

docs.title: For Most Environments
docs.text:
Use SSH proxy with localhost delegation:

# import-cluster.yml (no changes needed - already uses delegate_to: localhost)

# inventory/hosts.ini
[rhacm_hub]
hub-cluster kubeconfig_path=/path/to/hub-kubeconfig

[target_clusters]
prod-cluster-01 kubeconfig_path=/path/to/prod-cluster-01-kubeconfig

[target_clusters:vars]
ansible_ssh_common_args='-o ProxyJump=bastion.example.com'

docs.title: For Air-Gapped Environments
docs.text:
Install dependencies on bastion and modify delegation:

# import-cluster.yml - modify delegation target
- name: Create ManagedCluster resource on hub
  kubernetes.core.k8s:
    # ... config ...
  delegate_to: "{{ bastion_host | default('localhost') }}"

# inventory/hosts.ini
[bastion]
bastion.example.com ansible_user=admin

[target_clusters:vars]
bastion_host=bastion.example.com

docs.title: Check Python Installation
docs.text:
System-wide packages: 

# On the node executing tasks (bastion or localhost)
python3 --version
pip3 list | grep kubernetes
python3 -c "import kubernetes; print(kubernetes.__version__)"

User-specific packages: 

# Check user-installed packages
pip3 list --user | grep kubernetes

# Check installation location
python3 -c "import kubernetes; print(kubernetes.__file__)"
# Should show: /home/username/.local/lib/python3.x/site-packages/...

# Check Python path
python3 -c "import sys; print('\n'.join(sys.path))"

docs.title: User vs System Installation Issues
docs.text:
Problem: User installs package but Ansible can't find it

Cause: Ansible may run with different Python interpreter or PATH

Fix: Ensure user's .local/bin is in PATH 

# Add to ~/.bashrc or ~/.bash_profile
export PATH="$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH"

# Reload
source ~/.bashrc

Or specify Python interpreter in inventory: 

[bastion]
bastion.example.com ansible_python_interpreter=/usr/bin/python3

docs.title: Check Delegation Target
docs.text:
Add debug task to playbook:

- name: Debug delegation
  debug:
    msg:
      - "Delegated to: {{ inventory_hostname }}"
      - "Python path: {{ ansible_python_interpreter | default('python3') }}"
  delegate_to: localhost  # or your bastion

docs.title: Test kubernetes.core Module
docs.text:
# Create test playbook
cat > test-k8s.yml <<EOF
---
- hosts: localhost
  tasks:
    - name: Test kubernetes module
      kubernetes.core.k8s_info:
        kind: Namespace
        name: default
      register: result
    - debug: var=result
EOF

# Run test
ansible-playbook test-k8s.yml

docs.title: Common Errors and Fixes
docs.text:
Error: ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'kubernetes' 

pip3 install kubernetes

Error: No module named 'yaml' 

pip3 install PyYAML

Error: requests package required 

pip3 install requests

Error: cannot import name 'client' from 'kubernetes' 

# Version conflict - reinstall
pip3 uninstall kubernetes -y
pip3 install kubernetes

docs.title: SSH Proxy Approach (Recommended)
docs.text:
Ansible Control Node (localhost)
  ↓ (SSH via bastion)
Bastion Host (proxy only, no Python deps needed)
  ↓ (SSH tunnel)
Target Cluster API

docs.title: Bastion Delegation Approach
docs.text:
Ansible Control Node
  ↓ (SSH)
Bastion Host (Python + kubernetes library required)
  ↓ (Direct API call)
Hub/Target Cluster API

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Use SSH proxy when possible - Keeps dependencies on control node
  2. Document bastion requirements - If delegation required
  3. Version pin dependencies - In requirements.txt or ansible.cfg
  4. Test in non-prod first - Verify connectivity and permissions
  5. Automate bastion setup - Use bastion-setup.yml playbook

docs.text:

  • bastion-setup.yml - Bastion dependency installer
  • inventory/hosts.ini - Inventory configuration

docs.title: RHACM Hub Cluster RBAC Configuration
docs.text: This directory contains RBAC resources for creating a service account with minimal permissions to automate RHACM cluster imports.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Instead of using cluster-admin kubeconfig, create a dedicated service account with least-privilege permissions:

  • ✅ Create namespaces for imported clusters
  • ✅ Create ManagedCluster resources
  • ✅ Create KlusterletAddonConfig resources
  • ✅ Read import secrets (auto-generated by RHACM)
  • ✅ Read ManagedCluster status for validation
  • ❌ No permissions to modify unrelated resources
  • ❌ No permissions to delete clusters (safety)

docs.title: 1. Apply RBAC Resources to Hub Cluster
docs.text:
# Apply all RBAC configurations
oc apply -f serviceaccount.yaml
oc apply -f clusterrole.yaml
oc apply -f clusterrolebinding.yaml
oc apply -f namespace-role.yaml

Or apply all at once:

oc apply -f hub-rbac/

docs.title: 2. Extract Service Account Token
docs.text:
For OpenShift 4.11+ (using TokenRequest API):

#!/bin/bash
# extract-token.sh

SA_NAME="cluster-importer"
NAMESPACE="open-cluster-management"

# Create a long-lived token (1 year)
TOKEN=$(oc create token ${SA_NAME} -n ${NAMESPACE} --duration=8760h)

echo "Service account token:"
echo "$TOKEN"

# Save to file for Ansible
echo "$TOKEN" > /tmp/cluster-importer-token.txt
chmod 600 /tmp/cluster-importer-token.txt

echo ""
echo "Token saved to: /tmp/cluster-importer-token.txt"

For OpenShift 4.10 and earlier (using Secret-based tokens):

#!/bin/bash
# extract-token-legacy.sh

SA_NAME="cluster-importer"
NAMESPACE="open-cluster-management"

# Get the secret name
SECRET_NAME=$(oc get sa ${SA_NAME} -n ${NAMESPACE} \
  -o jsonpath='{.secrets[0].name}')

# Extract token
TOKEN=$(oc get secret ${SECRET_NAME} -n ${NAMESPACE} \
  -o jsonpath='{.data.token}' | base64 -d)

echo "Service account token:"
echo "$TOKEN"

# Save to file for Ansible
echo "$TOKEN" > /tmp/cluster-importer-token.txt
chmod 600 /tmp/cluster-importer-token.txt

echo ""
echo "Token saved to: /tmp/cluster-importer-token.txt"

docs.title: 3. Create Kubeconfig for Service Account
docs.text:
#!/bin/bash
# create-kubeconfig.sh

SA_NAME="cluster-importer"
NAMESPACE="open-cluster-management"
CLUSTER_NAME="rhacm-hub"  # Change to your hub cluster name
SERVER_URL=$(oc whoami --show-server)

# Extract CA certificate
CA_CERT=$(oc config view --raw -o jsonpath='{.clusters[0].cluster.certificate-authority-data}')

# Get token (use one of the methods above)
TOKEN=$(cat /tmp/cluster-importer-token.txt)

# Create kubeconfig
cat > /tmp/cluster-importer-kubeconfig <<EOF
apiVersion: v1
kind: Config
clusters:
  - cluster:
      certificate-authority-data: ${CA_CERT}
      server: ${SERVER_URL}
    name: ${CLUSTER_NAME}
contexts:
  - context:
      cluster: ${CLUSTER_NAME}
      namespace: ${NAMESPACE}
      user: ${SA_NAME}
    name: ${SA_NAME}@${CLUSTER_NAME}
current-context: ${SA_NAME}@${CLUSTER_NAME}
users:
  - name: ${SA_NAME}
    user:
      token: ${TOKEN}
EOF

chmod 600 /tmp/cluster-importer-kubeconfig

echo "Kubeconfig created: /tmp/cluster-importer-kubeconfig"
echo ""
echo "Test with:"
echo "  export KUBECONFIG=/tmp/cluster-importer-kubeconfig"
echo "  oc whoami"
echo "  oc auth can-i create managedcluster"

docs.title: 4. Update Ansible Inventory
docs.text:
Update inventory/hosts.ini to use the service account kubeconfig:

[rhacm_hub]
hub-cluster kubeconfig_path=/tmp/cluster-importer-kubeconfig

docs.title: 5. Test Permissions
docs.text:
# Set kubeconfig
export KUBECONFIG=/tmp/cluster-importer-kubeconfig

# Test basic access
oc whoami
# Expected: system:serviceaccount:open-cluster-management:cluster-importer

# Test permissions
oc auth can-i create managedcluster
# Expected: yes

oc auth can-i create namespace
# Expected: yes

oc auth can-i get secret -n test-cluster
# Expected: yes

oc auth can-i delete managedcluster
# Expected: no (by design - safety)

oc auth can-i create deployment
# Expected: no (not needed for cluster import)

docs.title: Files in This Directory
docs.text:
hub-rbac/
├── README.md                    # This file
├── serviceaccount.yaml          # ServiceAccount definition
├── clusterrole.yaml             # ClusterRole with import permissions
├── clusterrolebinding.yaml      # Bind ClusterRole to ServiceAccount
└── namespace-role.yaml          # Role for cluster namespace access

docs.title: ClusterRole: cluster-importer
docs.text:
Namespaces: - create, get, list, watch - Create namespaces for imported clusters

Secrets: - get, list, watch - Read import secrets generated by RHACM - Note: No create or delete - secrets are auto-generated

ManagedCluster (cluster.open-cluster-management.io): - create, get, list, watch, update, patch - Full lifecycle management - Status: get, list, watch - Read cluster status for validation

KlusterletAddonConfig (agent.open-cluster-management.io): - create, get, list, watch, update, patch - Configure cluster add-ons

docs.title: ClusterRole: cluster-importer-namespace
docs.text: Scoped to cluster namespaces: - Read secrets in cluster namespace - Manage KlusterletAddonConfig in cluster namespace - Read ConfigMaps if needed

docs.title: Token Management
docs.text:
OpenShift 4.11+ (Recommended): - Use short-lived tokens with TokenRequest API - Rotate tokens regularly (weekly/monthly) - Set appropriate duration based on usage: - CI/CD: 1-2 hours (--duration=2h) - Automation: 24 hours (--duration=24h) - Long-running: 1 week max (--duration=168h)

Token Rotation Script: 

#!/bin/bash
# rotate-token.sh

SA_NAME="cluster-importer"
NAMESPACE="open-cluster-management"

# Generate new token
NEW_TOKEN=$(oc create token ${SA_NAME} -n ${NAMESPACE} --duration=24h)

# Update kubeconfig (assumes standard structure)
KUBECONFIG_FILE="/path/to/cluster-importer-kubeconfig"
kubectl config set-credentials ${SA_NAME} --token="${NEW_TOKEN}" \
  --kubeconfig="${KUBECONFIG_FILE}"

echo "Token rotated successfully"

docs.title: Audit and Monitoring
docs.text:
Enable audit logging for service account actions:

# OpenShift audit policy (cluster-wide)
apiVersion: audit.k8s.io/v1
kind: Policy
rules:
  - level: RequestResponse
    users:
      - system:serviceaccount:open-cluster-management:cluster-importer
    verbs: ["create", "update", "patch", "delete"]

Monitor service account usage:

# View recent actions by service account
oc adm node-logs --role=master --path=kube-apiserver/audit.log | \
  grep "cluster-importer" | tail -20

docs.title: Least Privilege Principle
docs.text:
This configuration follows security best practices:

✅ Minimal Permissions: Only what's needed for cluster import ✅ No Delete: Can't accidentally delete clusters ✅ No Secrets Write: Can't create/modify secrets ✅ Scoped Access: Limited to RHACM-related resources ✅ Auditable: All actions logged with service account identity

docs.title: Integration with Vault/External Secrets
docs.text:
For production, store service account tokens in a secret manager:

HashiCorp Vault: 

# Store token in Vault
vault kv put secret/rhacm/cluster-importer \
  token="$(cat /tmp/cluster-importer-token.txt)" \
  server="https://api.hub.example.com:6443"

# Retrieve in Ansible
- name: Get hub token from Vault
  set_fact:
    hub_token: "{{ lookup('community.hashi_vault.hashi_vault_read', 
                          'secret/data/rhacm/cluster-importer').token }}"

AWS Secrets Manager: 

# Store token
aws secretsmanager create-secret \
  --name rhacm/cluster-importer-token \
  --secret-string file:///tmp/cluster-importer-token.txt

# Retrieve in Ansible
- name: Get hub token from AWS
  set_fact:
    hub_token: "{{ lookup('amazon.aws.aws_secret', 
                          'rhacm/cluster-importer-token') }}"

docs.title: Permission Denied Errors
docs.text:
Symptom: Playbook fails with "forbidden" errors

Check permissions: 

export KUBECONFIG=/tmp/cluster-importer-kubeconfig

# Test specific resource
oc auth can-i create managedcluster
oc auth can-i get secret -n test-namespace

# View effective permissions
oc auth can-i --list

Common causes: - ClusterRoleBinding not applied - Wrong namespace for ServiceAccount - Token expired (for short-lived tokens)

docs.title: Token Expired
docs.text:
Symptom: "Unauthorized" or "invalid authentication token"

Fix: 

# Generate new token
oc create token cluster-importer -n open-cluster-management \
  --duration=24h > /tmp/cluster-importer-token.txt

# Update kubeconfig
./create-kubeconfig.sh

docs.title: ServiceAccount Not Found
docs.text:
Symptom: "serviceaccounts 'cluster-importer' not found"

Fix: 

# Verify ServiceAccount exists
oc get sa cluster-importer -n open-cluster-management

# If not, create it
oc apply -f serviceaccount.yaml

docs.title: Missing Namespace Permissions
docs.text:
Symptom: Can't read secrets in cluster namespace

Fix: 

# Create RoleBinding for specific cluster namespace
cat <<EOF | oc apply -f -
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: RoleBinding
metadata:
  name: cluster-importer
  namespace: prod-cluster-01
roleRef:
  apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
  kind: ClusterRole
  name: cluster-importer-namespace
subjects:
  - kind: ServiceAccount
    name: cluster-importer
    namespace: open-cluster-management
EOF

docs.title: Restrict to Specific Namespaces
docs.text:
If you want to limit which cluster namespaces the service account can access:

# Replace ClusterRole with multiple Roles
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: Role
metadata:
  name: cluster-importer
  namespace: prod-cluster-01  # Specific cluster namespace
rules:
  # Same rules as cluster-importer-namespace
---
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: RoleBinding
metadata:
  name: cluster-importer
  namespace: prod-cluster-01
roleRef:
  apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
  kind: Role
  name: cluster-importer
subjects:
  - kind: ServiceAccount
    name: cluster-importer
    namespace: open-cluster-management

docs.title: Add ManagedClusterSet Management
docs.text:
To automatically assign clusters to sets, uncomment these lines in clusterrole.yaml:

- apiGroups: ["cluster.open-cluster-management.io"]
  resources: ["managedclustersets"]
  verbs: ["get", "list", "watch"]

- apiGroups: ["cluster.open-cluster-management.io"]
  resources: ["managedclustersets/join"]
  verbs: ["create"]

Then add to your playbook:

- name: Add cluster to ManagedClusterSet
  kubernetes.core.k8s:
    kubeconfig: "{{ hub_kubeconfig }}"
    state: present
    definition:
      apiVersion: cluster.open-cluster-management.io/v1beta2
      kind: ManagedClusterSetBinding
      metadata:
        name: production-clusters
        namespace: "{{ cluster_name }}"
      spec:
        clusterSet: production-clusters

docs.title: Troubleshooting RBAC for hubAcceptsClient
docs.text: This guide helps diagnose and fix RBAC issues when creating ManagedCluster resources with hubAcceptsClient: true.

docs.title: The Error
docs.text:
admission webhook "managedclustervalidators.admission.cluster.open-cluster-management.io" 
denied the request: managedclusters/accept "cluster-name" is forbidden: 
user "system:serviceaccount:open-cluster-management:cluster-importer" 
cannot update the HubAcceptsClient field

docs.title: Root Cause
docs.text: The hubAcceptsClient field is protected by RHACM's admission webhook and requires permission to update the managedclusters/accept subresource. The exact API group for this subresource can vary by RHACM version.

docs.title: Step 1: Run the Debug Script
docs.text:
cd hub-rbac/

# Using service account kubeconfig
export KUBECONFIG=/tmp/cluster-importer-kubeconfig
./debug-rbac.sh

Look for the output section:

3. Testing permissions for service account...
  ✗ can-i update managedclusters/accept (denied)

docs.title: Step 2: Check API Resources
docs.text:
# See what API resources exist on your hub cluster
kubectl api-resources | grep managedcluster

# Expected output might include:
# managedclusters    cluster.open-cluster-management.io
# managedclusters    register.open-cluster-management.io

docs.title: Step 3: Verify ClusterRole is Applied
docs.text:
# Check ClusterRole exists
oc get clusterrole cluster-importer

# Check it has the accept permission
oc get clusterrole cluster-importer -o yaml | grep -A 5 "managedclusters/accept"

# Expected output:
#   - apiGroups: ["cluster.open-cluster-management.io"]
#     resources: ["managedclusters/accept"]
#     verbs: ["update"]
#   - apiGroups: ["register.open-cluster-management.io"]
#     resources: ["managedclusters/accept"]
#     verbs: ["update"]

docs.title: Step 4: Verify ClusterRoleBinding
docs.text:
# Check binding exists
oc get clusterrolebinding cluster-importer

# Verify it points to correct service account
oc get clusterrolebinding cluster-importer -o yaml

# Expected:
# subjects:
#   - kind: ServiceAccount
#     name: cluster-importer
#     namespace: open-cluster-management

docs.title: Step 5: Test Permission Directly
docs.text:
# Test as the service account
kubectl auth can-i update managedclusters/accept \
  --as=system:serviceaccount:open-cluster-management:cluster-importer \
  -n test-cluster

# Should return: yes

docs.title: Solution 1: Use Extended ClusterRole
docs.text:
If the basic ClusterRole doesn't work, try the extended version:

# Remove old binding (keeps ClusterRole)
oc delete clusterrolebinding cluster-importer

# Apply extended versions
oc apply -f clusterrole-extended.yaml
oc apply -f clusterrolebinding-extended.yaml

# Regenerate kubeconfig (to pick up new permissions)
./extract-token.sh
./create-kubeconfig.sh

# Test again
./debug-rbac.sh

The extended ClusterRole includes: - Both API groups for accept subresource - CSR approval permissions - ManagedClusterSet permissions - Work API permissions

docs.title: Solution 2: Check RHACM Version Specific Requirements
docs.text:
Different RHACM versions may have different requirements. Check your version:

# Check RHACM version
oc get csv -n open-cluster-management | grep advanced-cluster-management

# Check multicluster-engine version
oc get csv -n multicluster-engine | grep multicluster-engine

Version-specific notes:

RHACM 2.5-2.7: - Uses cluster.open-cluster-management.io for most operations - May require register.open-cluster-management.io for accept

RHACM 2.8+: - Multicluster Engine (MCE) handles cluster lifecycle - May require additional work API permissions

docs.title: Solution 3: Check for Admission Webhook Issues
docs.text:
# Check if admission webhooks are healthy
oc get validatingwebhookconfigurations | grep managedcluster

# Check specific webhook
oc get validatingwebhookconfigurations \
  managedclustervalidators.admission.cluster.open-cluster-management.io -o yaml

# Check webhook pod
oc get pods -n open-cluster-management | grep webhook
oc logs -n open-cluster-management <webhook-pod>

docs.title: Solution 4: Verify Service Account Token is Fresh
docs.text:
Stale tokens may not have latest permissions:

# Regenerate token
cd hub-rbac/
./extract-token.sh

# Recreate kubeconfig
./create-kubeconfig.sh

# Test permissions
export KUBECONFIG=/tmp/cluster-importer-kubeconfig
oc auth can-i update managedclusters/accept

docs.title: Solution 5: Try Manual Creation with Service Account
docs.text:
Test directly without Ansible:

export KUBECONFIG=/tmp/cluster-importer-kubeconfig

# Try creating a ManagedCluster
oc create -f - <<EOF
apiVersion: cluster.open-cluster-management.io/v1
kind: ManagedCluster
metadata:
  name: test-rbac-manual
  labels:
    environment: test
spec:
  hubAcceptsClient: true
  leaseDurationSeconds: 60
EOF

If this succeeds: Ansible playbook has an issue, not RBAC If this fails: RBAC needs more permissions

docs.title: Finding 1: Wrong API Group
docs.text:
Symptom: Permission denied even after adding accept subresource

Solution: The API group varies by version. Run: 

# Check API versions
oc api-versions | grep cluster-management
oc api-versions | grep register

# Output might show:
# cluster.open-cluster-management.io/v1
# register.open-cluster-management.io/v1

Use whichever group(s) appear in your output.

docs.title: Finding 2: CSR Approval Required
docs.text:
Symptom: Cluster joins but never becomes available

Solution: Add CSR permissions (included in extended ClusterRole)

docs.title: Finding 3: Webhook Certificate Issues
docs.text:
Symptom: Webhook errors in logs

Solution: Check webhook certificates: 

oc get validatingwebhookconfigurations -o yaml | grep caBundle

docs.title: Quick Test Matrix
docs.text:
Run these tests in order to narrow down the issue:

Test Command Expected If Fails 1. Basic auth oc whoami service account name Fix kubeconfig 2. Namespace create oc auth can-i create namespace yes Fix ClusterRole 3. ManagedCluster create oc auth can-i create managedcluster yes Fix ClusterRole 4. Accept permission oc auth can-i update managedclusters/accept yes Use extended role 5. Dry-run create oc create -f test.yaml --dry-run=server success Check webhook

docs.title: Fallback Option 1: Use Cluster-Admin Group
docs.text:
Add service account to cluster-admin (not recommended for production):

oc adm policy add-cluster-role-to-user cluster-admin \
  system:serviceaccount:open-cluster-management:cluster-importer

docs.title: Fallback Option 2: Copy Existing RHACM Role
docs.text:
RHACM has built-in roles that work. Copy their permissions:

# Find RHACM's own cluster import role
oc get clusterrole | grep -i cluster | grep -i import

# Examine it
oc get clusterrole <rhacm-role-name> -o yaml

# Use those permissions as reference

docs.title: Still Stuck?
docs.text:
Share the output of:

cd hub-rbac/
./debug-rbac.sh > rbac-debug-output.txt 2>&1

# Also get ClusterRole details
oc get clusterrole cluster-importer -o yaml >> rbac-debug-output.txt

# And webhook configuration
oc get validatingwebhookconfigurations \
  managedclustervalidators.admission.cluster.open-cluster-management.io \
  -o yaml >> rbac-debug-output.txt 2>&1 || echo "Webhook not found" >> rbac-debug-output.txt

Share rbac-debug-output.txt for further analysis.

Last Updated: February 19, 2026

docs.title: RHACM → ArgoCD Cluster Integration
docs.text: This pattern registers RHACM-managed clusters with an OpenShift GitOps (ArgoCD) instance using the ClusterSet-based integration. Clusters added to the ClusterSet are automatically discovered and made available as ArgoCD destinations — no manual secret creation required.

docs.title: Resources
docs.text:
File Kind Purpose managedclustersetbinding.yaml ManagedClusterSetBinding Grants openshift-gitops namespace access to the default ClusterSet placement.yaml Placement Selects all OpenShift clusters from that ClusterSet gitopscluster.yaml GitOpsCluster Registers selected clusters with ArgoCD

See also: ../argocd-rbac/ for the RHACM Policy that grants ArgoCD cluster-admin on each registered cluster.

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text:
ManagedClusterSet (default)
        │
        │  contains
        ▼
ManagedCluster (local-cluster, cluster-a, cluster-b, ...)
        │
        │  selected by
        ▼
Placement (all-openshift-clusters)   ◄── ManagedClusterSetBinding
        │                                 (allows openshift-gitops ns
        │  feeds into                      to use "default" set)
        ▼
GitOpsCluster (argo-acm-clusters)
        │
        │  creates cluster secret in
        ▼
openshift-gitops namespace
  └── <cluster-name>-cluster-secret  (Opaque)
        │
        │  registered as destination in
        ▼
ArgoCD — cluster available for ApplicationSet / Application targeting

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• RHACM MultiClusterHub in Running state
  • OpenShift GitOps operator installed (openshift-gitops namespace exists)
  • managed-serviceaccount addon enabled on target clusters (enabled by default with ACM 2.9+)
  • Target clusters added to the default ManagedClusterSet

docs.title: Apply
docs.text:
oc apply -f managedclustersetbinding.yaml
oc apply -f placement.yaml
oc apply -f gitopscluster.yaml

Or all at once:

oc apply -f .

docs.title: Verify
docs.text:
Check GitOpsCluster registered successfully:

oc get gitopscluster argo-acm-clusters -n openshift-gitops
# STATUS should be: successful

Check cluster secrets were created in the ArgoCD namespace:

oc get secret -n openshift-gitops -l argocd.argoproj.io/secret-type=cluster

You should see one secret per registered cluster (e.g. local-cluster-cluster-secret).

docs.title: Adding More Clusters
docs.text:
1. Import the new cluster into RHACM
  2. Label it with cluster.open-cluster-management.io/clusterset: default (or move it to the default set via the RHACM console)
  3. The Placement and GitOpsCluster will automatically pick it up — no changes to these manifests needed

docs.title: Narrowing Cluster Scope
docs.text:
To target only a subset of clusters, update the Placement predicates. Examples:

By environment label: 

predicates:
- requiredClusterSelector:
    labelSelector:
      matchLabels:
        environment: production

By cluster name: 

predicates:
- requiredClusterSelector:
    claimSelector:
      matchExpressions:
      - key: id.openshift.io
        operator: In
        values:
        - cluster-a
        - cluster-b

docs.title: OCM Subscription Automation
docs.text: Target Audience: Platform Engineers, Cluster Administrators Use Case: Bare metal OpenShift cluster post-install subscription configuration Last Updated: March 2026

docs.title: Problem Statement
docs.text:
After a bare metal OpenShift cluster is installed and registers with Red Hat, an administrator must manually visit console.redhat.com/openshift/cluster-list to configure subscription properties:

  1. Select Premium (support level)
  2. Select Red Hat Support (L1-L3) (SLA)
  3. Select Production or Development/Test (usage type)
  4. Select Cores or vCPUs (billing unit)
  5. Click Save
  6. Refresh the cluster web console to verify the SLA shows Premium Support Agreement

This is manual, error-prone, and does not scale across many clusters. This guide documents two automation approaches and introduces ClusterCurator as the next evolution for bare metal lifecycle automation.

docs.title: OCM CLI
docs.text:
# Download latest release
curl -Lo ocm https://github.com/openshift-online/ocm-cli/releases/latest/download/ocm-linux-amd64
chmod +x ocm
sudo mv ocm /usr/local/bin/

# Verify
ocm version

docs.title: Red Hat Offline Token
docs.text:
Generate a long-lived token at console.redhat.com/openshift/token.

This is not the pull secret. It is a separate OAuth token scoped to your Red Hat account for API access.

# Store securely - do not commit to Git
echo "your-token-here" > ~/rh-offline-token.txt
chmod 600 ~/rh-offline-token.txt

docs.title: python3
docs.text: Required for JSON parsing in the scripts. Available by default on RHEL/Fedora.

docs.title: Option 1: OCM CLI (Interactive / One-Off)
docs.text: Use this approach for ad-hoc changes, debugging, or verifying subscription state.

docs.title: Step 1 — Authenticate
docs.text: ocm login --token="$(cat ~/rh-offline-token.txt)"

docs.title: Step 2 — Find the Cluster
docs.text:
# List all clusters registered to your account
ocm list clusters

# Look up by name
ocm get /api/clusters_mgmt/v1/clusters \
  --parameter "search=name='prod-bm-01'" | python3 -m json.tool

# Get the cluster's OCM internal ID
CLUSTER_ID=$(ocm get /api/clusters_mgmt/v1/clusters \
  --parameter "search=name='prod-bm-01'" | \
  python3 -c "import sys,json; print(json.load(sys.stdin)['items'][0]['id'])")

echo "Cluster ID: $CLUSTER_ID"

docs.title: Step 3 — Find the Subscription
docs.text:
SUB_ID=$(ocm get /api/accounts_mgmt/v1/subscriptions \
  --parameter "search=cluster_id='${CLUSTER_ID}'" | \
  python3 -c "import sys,json; print(json.load(sys.stdin)['items'][0]['id'])")

echo "Subscription ID: $SUB_ID"

docs.title: Step 4 — View Current Subscription Settings
docs.text:
ocm get /api/accounts_mgmt/v1/subscriptions/${SUB_ID} | \
  python3 -c "
import sys, json
d = json.load(sys.stdin)
for field in ['support_level', 'service_level', 'usage', 'system_units']:
    print(f'{field:20s}: {d.get(field, \"not set\")}')
"

docs.title: Step 5 — Apply Settings
docs.text:
ocm patch /api/accounts_mgmt/v1/subscriptions/${SUB_ID} \
  --body='{
    "support_level": "Premium",
    "service_level": "L1-L3",
    "usage":         "Production",
    "system_units":  "Cores/vCPU"
  }'

docs.title: Step 6 — Verify
docs.text:
ocm get /api/accounts_mgmt/v1/subscriptions/${SUB_ID} | \
  python3 -c "
import sys, json
d = json.load(sys.stdin)
print('support_level :', d.get('support_level'))
print('service_level :', d.get('service_level'))
print('usage         :', d.get('usage'))
print('system_units  :', d.get('system_units'))
"

Then refresh the cluster's OpenShift web console and verify the SLA shows Premium Support Agreement.

docs.title: Option 2: Standalone Script (set-ocm-subscription.sh)
docs.text: Use this approach to automate the process in a CI/CD pipeline, Ansible playbook, or post-install hook.

docs.title: Script Location
docs.text: rhacm/examples/ocm-subscription-automation/set-ocm-subscription.sh

docs.title: Usage Examples
docs.text:
# Standard Premium Production cluster (enterprise default)
./set-ocm-subscription.sh \
  --cluster-name prod-bm-01 \
  --token-file ~/rh-offline-token.txt

# Development/Test cluster with Standard support
./set-ocm-subscription.sh \
  --cluster-name dev-bm-01 \
  --token-file ~/rh-offline-token.txt \
  --support-level Standard \
  --service-level L3 \
  --usage "Development/Test"

# Dry run to preview changes without applying
./set-ocm-subscription.sh \
  --cluster-name prod-bm-01 \
  --token-file ~/rh-offline-token.txt \
  --dry-run

# Use cluster ID directly (skips name lookup, faster)
./set-ocm-subscription.sh \
  --cluster-id abc-123-def-456 \
  --token "$(cat ~/rh-offline-token.txt)"

docs.title: Script Options
docs.text: Option Description Default --cluster-name NAME Cluster name in OCM (required) --cluster-id ID OCM cluster ID (skips lookup) (required if no name) --token TOKEN Offline token string (required) --token-file FILE Path to token file (required if no token) --support-level Premium, Standard, Self-Support, None Premium --service-level L1-L3, L3 L1-L3 --usage Production, Development/Test Production --system-units Cores/vCPU, Sockets Cores/vCPU --dry-run Preview changes without applying false --verbose Show debug output false

docs.title: Sample Output
docs.text:
[INFO]  Authenticating with Red Hat OCM...
[INFO]  Authenticated successfully
[INFO]  Looking up cluster: prod-bm-01
[INFO]  Target cluster ID: abc-123-def-456
[INFO]  Looking up subscription for cluster...

  ┌──────────────────┬──────────────────────┬──────────────────────┐
  │ Field            │ Current              │ Desired              │
  ├──────────────────┼──────────────────────┼──────────────────────┤
  │ support_level    │ Self-Support         │ Premium              │

docs.title: Integrate into a Pipeline
docs.text:
#!/bin/bash
# post-install.sh — Called after bare metal cluster install completes

CLUSTER_NAME="$1"
TOKEN_FILE="/etc/rh-credentials/ocm-token"

echo "Setting OCM subscription for: $CLUSTER_NAME"
/opt/scripts/set-ocm-subscription.sh \
  --cluster-name "$CLUSTER_NAME" \
  --token-file "$TOKEN_FILE" \
  --support-level Premium \
  --usage Production

docs.title: Store the Token as a Kubernetes Secret (for RHACM Hub)
docs.text:
# Create secret on RHACM hub for automation use
oc create secret generic rh-ocm-token \
  --from-file=token=~/rh-offline-token.txt \
  -n open-cluster-management

# Reference it in automation jobs
oc get secret rh-ocm-token -n open-cluster-management \
  -o jsonpath='{.data.token}' | base64 -d

docs.title: OCM Subscription Field Reference
docs.text: Console Label API Field Valid Values Support Level support_level Premium, Standard, Self-Support, None SLA service_level L1-L3, L3 Usage usage Production, Development/Test Billing Unit system_units Cores/vCPU, Sockets

docs.title: Field Meanings
docs.text:
support_level — Determines the entitlement tier: - Premium — Full enterprise support, 24x7 access, fastest response times - Standard — Business hours support - Self-Support — Portal access only, no case support - None — Evaluation/trial

service_level — Response time SLA: - L1-L3 — Red Hat handles L1 (basic), L2 (troubleshooting), and L3 (engineering escalation) - L3 — Customer handles L1/L2; Red Hat handles L3 engineering escalations only

usage — How the cluster is classified for entitlement purposes: - Production — Running live workloads - Development/Test — Non-production use; may affect entitlement counting

system_units — How cluster capacity is measured for subscription counting: - Cores/vCPU — Count by CPU cores or virtual CPUs (most common for bare metal) - Sockets — Count by physical CPU sockets (legacy licensing model)

docs.title: What is ClusterCurator?
docs.text:
See cluster-curator/README.md for a detailed explanation of ClusterCurator and how it enables automatic post-install subscription configuration for bare metal clusters.

Short answer: ClusterCurator is an RHACM component that lets you run pre- and post-install automation hooks (Ansible jobs) around cluster lifecycle events — provisioning, upgrading, scaling, and decommissioning. For bare metal, it eliminates the need to manually trigger the OCM subscription script after each cluster install.

docs.title: "Cluster not found in OCM"
docs.text:
The cluster may not have phoned home yet. Check:

# On the cluster — is insights-operator running?
oc get clusteroperator insights
oc get pods -n openshift-insights

# Is the pull secret valid?
oc get secret pull-secret -n openshift-config \
  -o jsonpath='{.data.\.dockerconfigjson}' | base64 -d | \
  python3 -m json.tool | grep -A2 "cloud.openshift.com"

docs.title: "No subscription found for cluster ID"
docs.text:
The cluster is registered but no subscription is attached. This happens when: - The cluster was installed with a personal/developer Red Hat account that has no OCP entitlement - The subscription was not yet propagated from Red Hat's backend

Contact your Red Hat account team or open a support case to manually attach the subscription.

docs.title: "support_level mismatch after patch"
docs.text:
Your Red Hat account may not have the Premium entitlement. Verify quota:

ocm get /api/accounts_mgmt/v1/quota_summary

docs.title: OCM CLI Authentication Fails
docs.text:
# Re-generate token at:
# https://console.redhat.com/openshift/token
# Then re-login:
ocm logout
ocm login --token="$(cat ~/rh-offline-token.txt)"

docs.title: ClusterCurator — Education Guide for Bare Metal
docs.text:
Target Audience: Platform Engineers not yet using ClusterCurator Context: Bare metal OpenShift clusters managed by RHACM Last Updated: March 2026

See also: agent-install-preflight.md — where prehooks fit in the full agent install lifecycle (validations, approval gates, external pipelines). See also: acm-ansible-integration.md — all native ACM→Ansible paths, AAP vs AWX, and prerequisites. See also: bare-metal-lifecycle-hook-patterns.md — implementation patterns (AAP, Go, operator, CI) with examples and pros/cons.

docs.title: What is ClusterCurator?
docs.text:
ClusterCurator is an RHACM component (part of the cluster-curator-controller) that lets you run automated pre- and post-hooks around cluster lifecycle events:

  • Provisioning a new cluster (install)
  • Upgrading a cluster
  • Scaling a cluster (adding/removing nodes)
  • Destroying a cluster (decommission)

Hooks run as Ansible jobs (via Ansible Automation Platform or AWX) or as directly invoked scripts. This makes ClusterCurator the glue between cluster infrastructure events and your operational automation.

docs.title: Without ClusterCurator (Current State)
docs.text:
Install cluster → Cluster becomes available → Engineer manually:
                                               1. Logs into console.redhat.com
                                               2. Finds cluster
                                               3. Sets subscription properties
                                               4. Verifies in web console

docs.title: With ClusterCurator (Target State)
docs.text:
Install cluster → Cluster becomes available → ClusterCurator automatically:
                                               1. Calls Ansible job
                                               2. Ansible runs set-ocm-subscription.sh
                                               3. Subscription is set
                                               4. Notification sent to team

docs.title: Components
docs.text:
RHACM Hub Cluster
├── cluster-curator-controller       # Watches ClusterCurator CRDs
├── ClusterCurator CRD               # Per-cluster lifecycle automation config
└── AnsibleJob CRD                   # Generated by curator to invoke automation
         │
         ▼
Ansible Automation Platform (AAP) / AWX
└── Job Templates                    # Your playbooks that run pre/post hooks
         │
         ▼
Post-Install Automation
└── set-ocm-subscription.sh          # Your OCM subscription script

docs.title: ClusterCurator CRD
docs.text:
The ClusterCurator resource lives in the same namespace as the cluster on the hub. It defines what automation to run at each lifecycle stage.

apiVersion: cluster.open-cluster-management.io/v1beta1
kind: ClusterCurator
metadata:
  name: prod-bm-01                   # Must match the cluster name
  namespace: prod-bm-01              # Must match the cluster namespace
spec:
  desiredCuration: install           # Trigger: install | upgrade | scale | destroy
  install:
    prehook:
      - name: validate-network       # AAP Job Template name
        extra_vars:
          cluster_name: prod-bm-01
    posthook:
      - name: set-ocm-subscription   # AAP Job Template name
        extra_vars:
          cluster_name: prod-bm-01
          support_level: Premium
          usage: Production
  towerAuthSecret: aap-credentials   # Secret with AAP/AWX credentials

docs.title: Lifecycle Stages
docs.text:
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                  Cluster Install Flow                     │
├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  ClusterCurator.spec.install.prehook                     │
│  └─ Ansible jobs run BEFORE installation starts          │
│     (e.g. validate DNS, reserve IP, create CMDB record)  │
│                         │                                │
│                         ▼                                │
│  Cluster Installation (Assisted Installer / Hive)        │
│                         │                                │
│                         ▼                                │
│  ClusterCurator.spec.install.posthook                    │
│  └─ Ansible jobs run AFTER installation completes        │
│     (e.g. set OCM subscription, notify team, setup LDAP) │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

docs.title: Bare Metal Use Case: Post-Install API Cert + ACM Trust Sync
docs.text:
When custom API serving certificates are applied after CIM install, ACM hub kubeconfig and klusterlet trust must be refreshed or clusters show x509: certificate signed by unknown authority.

Draft reference implementation:

  • postinstall-api-cert-acm-sync/README.md — ClusterCurator posthook, AAP playbook, cert manifests
  • custom-api-certs-and-acm-trust.md — Peer share: GitOps + Argo two-app PostSync pattern (recommended for cert-manager fleets)
  • Troubleshooting when this was not automated: managed-cluster-x509-after-api-cert-change.md

docs.title: Bare Metal Use Case: OCM Subscription via ClusterCurator
What You Need
docs.text:
1. Ansible Automation Platform (AAP) or AWX connected to RHACM
  2. Job Template in AAP with a playbook that calls the OCM subscription script
  3. ClusterCurator resource deployed alongside each cluster

docs.title: Step 1 — Store OCM Token as Kubernetes Secret on Hub
docs.text:
oc create secret generic rh-ocm-token \
  --from-file=token=/path/to/offline-token.txt \
  -n open-cluster-management

docs.title: Step 2 — Create AAP Credentials Secret on Hub
docs.text:
oc create secret generic aap-credentials \
  --from-literal=host=https://aap.example.com \
  --from-literal=token=<aap-api-token> \
  -n prod-bm-01

The secret structure ClusterCurator expects:

apiVersion: v1
kind: Secret
metadata:
  name: aap-credentials
  namespace: prod-bm-01
type: Opaque
stringData:
  host: "https://aap.example.com"
  token: "your-aap-api-token"

docs.title: Step 3 — Create the Ansible Playbook (in AAP)
docs.text:
This playbook runs on the RHACM hub (or a jump host) and calls the subscription script:

# playbook: set-ocm-subscription.yml
---
- name: Set OCM subscription for new cluster
  hosts: localhost
  gather_facts: false
  vars:
    cluster_name: "{{ cluster_name }}"
    support_level: "{{ support_level | default('Premium') }}"
    service_level: "{{ service_level | default('L1-L3') }}"
    usage: "{{ usage | default('Production') }}"
    system_units: "{{ system_units | default('Cores/vCPU') }}"

  tasks:
    - name: Retrieve OCM token from Kubernetes secret
      kubernetes.core.k8s_info:
        api_version: v1
        kind: Secret
        name: rh-ocm-token
        namespace: open-cluster-management
      register: ocm_secret

    - name: Set OCM token fact
      ansible.builtin.set_fact:
        ocm_token: "{{ ocm_secret.resources[0].data.token | b64decode }}"

    - name: Login to OCM
      ansible.builtin.command:
        cmd: "ocm login --token={{ ocm_token }}"
      no_log: true

    - name: Get cluster ID from OCM
      ansible.builtin.shell: |
        ocm get /api/clusters_mgmt/v1/clusters \
          --parameter "search=name='{{ cluster_name }}'" | \
          python3 -c "import sys,json; print(json.load(sys.stdin)['items'][0]['id'])"
      register: cluster_id_result

    - name: Get subscription ID
      ansible.builtin.shell: |
        ocm get /api/accounts_mgmt/v1/subscriptions \
          --parameter "search=cluster_id='{{ cluster_id_result.stdout }}'" | \
          python3 -c "import sys,json; print(json.load(sys.stdin)['items'][0]['id'])"
      register: sub_id_result

    - name: Patch subscription settings
      ansible.builtin.shell: |
        ocm patch /api/accounts_mgmt/v1/subscriptions/{{ sub_id_result.stdout }} \
          --body='{{ payload | to_json }}'
      vars:
        payload:
          support_level: "{{ support_level }}"
          service_level: "{{ service_level }}"
          usage: "{{ usage }}"
          system_units: "{{ system_units }}"

    - name: Confirm settings applied
      ansible.builtin.debug:
        msg: "OCM subscription configured for {{ cluster_name }}: {{ support_level }} / {{ usage }}"

docs.title: Step 4 — Create the ClusterCurator Resource
docs.text:
Apply this to the RHACM hub alongside your cluster deployment:

apiVersion: cluster.open-cluster-management.io/v1beta1
kind: ClusterCurator
metadata:
  name: prod-bm-01
  namespace: prod-bm-01
spec:
  desiredCuration: install
  install:
    prehook: []                          # No pre-install automation yet
    posthook:
      - name: set-ocm-subscription       # Job Template name in AAP
        extra_vars:
          cluster_name: prod-bm-01
          support_level: Premium
          service_level: L1-L3
          usage: Production
          system_units: Cores/vCPU
  towerAuthSecret: aap-credentials

docs.title: Step 5 — Monitor Execution
docs.text:
# Watch ClusterCurator status
oc get clustercurator prod-bm-01 -n prod-bm-01 -w

# View generated AnsibleJob
oc get ansiblejob -n prod-bm-01

# Describe for details
oc describe clustercurator prod-bm-01 -n prod-bm-01

docs.title: ClusterCurator Without AAP (Direct Script Invocation)
docs.text:
If you are not yet using Ansible Automation Platform, ClusterCurator can invoke hooks as Kubernetes Jobs instead. This is a lighter-weight approach suitable for getting started.

Note: Direct job execution (without AAP) requires a custom operator setup and is less commonly documented. The AAP integration is the primary supported path. If AAP is not available, the standalone script run from a CI/CD pipeline (Tekton, Jenkins, GitHub Actions) is the practical alternative.

docs.title: Practical Alternative: Tekton Pipeline as Post-Install Hook
docs.text:
# tekton/post-install-pipeline.yaml
apiVersion: tekton.dev/v1beta1
kind: Pipeline
metadata:
  name: post-cluster-install
  namespace: open-cluster-management
spec:
  params:
    - name: cluster-name
    - name: support-level
      default: Premium
    - name: usage
      default: Production
  tasks:
    - name: set-ocm-subscription
      taskRef:
        name: run-ocm-subscription-script
      params:
        - name: cluster-name
          value: $(params.cluster-name)
        - name: support-level
          value: $(params.support-level)
        - name: usage
          value: $(params.usage)

docs.title: ClusterCurator for Full Bare Metal Lifecycle
docs.text:
Once you are comfortable with post-install hooks, expand to the full lifecycle:

apiVersion: cluster.open-cluster-management.io/v1beta1
kind: ClusterCurator
metadata:
  name: prod-bm-01
  namespace: prod-bm-01
spec:
  desiredCuration: install
  install:
    prehook:
      - name: validate-dns-entries         # Verify DNS before install
          extra_vars:
            api_vip: 10.20.30.10
            ingress_vip: 10.20.30.11
            cluster_name: prod-bm-01
      - name: create-cmdb-record           # Register in asset management
          extra_vars:
            cluster_name: prod-bm-01
            environment: production
    posthook:
      - name: set-ocm-subscription         # Set Red Hat subscription
          extra_vars:
            cluster_name: prod-bm-01
            support_level: Premium
      - name: configure-ldap-auth          # Set up LDAP authentication
          extra_vars:
            cluster_name: prod-bm-01
      - name: notify-teams-channel         # Alert team in Slack/Teams
          extra_vars:
            cluster_name: prod-bm-01
            message: "Cluster prod-bm-01 is ready"
  upgrade:
    prehook:
      - name: pre-upgrade-health-check
    posthook:
      - name: post-upgrade-validation
  destroy:
    prehook:
      - name: backup-etcd
      - name: notify-decommission
    posthook:
      - name: remove-cmdb-record
      - name: release-ip-reservations
      - name: wipe-bare-metal-disks   # custom AAP job — see rhacm/notes/bare-metal-cluster-destroy.md
  towerAuthSecret: aap-credentials

For what RHACM destroy does and does not do on bare metal (disk wipe is not built-in), see bare-metal-cluster-destroy.md and Bare Metal RHCOS Disk Wipe.

docs.title: Comparison: Current vs. ClusterCurator
docs.text: Aspect Current (Manual / Script) With ClusterCurator Trigger Manual after install Automatic on cluster ready Operator Human runs script RHACM controller triggers job Scale One at a time All clusters automatically Auditability Shell history AnsibleJob resources + AAP logs Error handling Manual retry AAP retry logic Extensibility Shell script only Any Ansible playbook GitOps Script in repo ClusterCurator CRD in Git

docs.title: Getting Started with ClusterCurator — Recommended Path
Phase 1 (Now): Standalone Script
docs.text: Run set-ocm-subscription.sh manually or from your CI/CD pipeline after each cluster install. Low setup cost, immediate benefit.

docs.title: Phase 2 (Next): ClusterCurator + AAP
docs.text: Once you have AAP deployed, convert the standalone script into an Ansible playbook and create ClusterCurator resources alongside each cluster deployment.

docs.title: Phase 3 (Future): Full Lifecycle Automation
docs.text: Expand prehooks and posthooks to cover DNS validation, CMDB registration, LDAP configuration, notifications, and decommission workflows.

docs.title: Checking ClusterCurator Is Available
docs.text:
# Check if cluster-curator-controller is installed
oc get deployment cluster-curator-controller -n open-cluster-management

# Check CRD is present
oc get crd clustercurators.cluster.open-cluster-management.io

# View existing ClusterCurators
oc get clustercurator --all-namespaces

If the controller is not present, it ships with RHACM 2.2+ and should be installed by default. Check your MCE/RHACM operator subscription.
